newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko reacts coolly to EU report on Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko reacts coolly to EU report on Belarus.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko said on Monday a report on his country by the European Union was "one-sided" and defended a much-criticised referendum that has given him sweeping new powers.

The EU report has not been published, but in a statement issued after Lukashenko received a copy from visiting EU officials the presidential press service said: "Some of the report's conclusions were one-sided."
"President Lukashenko emphasised (to the EU delegation) that the will of the Belarussian people, as expressed in the referendum, should be respected," the statement added.
The report was drawn up in response to the referendum last November which authorised Lukashenko to take broad powers and rewrite the former Soviet republic's constitution.

The EU, the Council of Europe and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) all criticised the referendum and said Lukashenko's new constitution fails to meet minimum standards on human rights.
Last Friday the U.S. State Department accused Belarus of failing to uphold democracy and human rights and announced it was halting all U.S. aid to the country of 10 million.
The EU has said it will publish its report in due course if Lukashenko refuses to accept its recommendations.
The Belarussian Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Monday that the report did not touch on human rights or press freedom but concentrated on the judicial aspects of Lukashenko's referendum.

In Moscow, the European Commissioner in charge of relations with eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, Hans van den Broek, said the EU wanted better relations with Minsk but added that the Belarussian authorities were not being cooperative.
"There are a number of political circumstances of a domestic nature there that hamper the full development of good relations," he told reporters after talks with Russian leaders.

Lukashenko, who wants closer ties with Moscow, is expected to meet President Boris Yeltsin in the Kremlin on Friday for talks on how to speed up integration following last year's agreement to create a "community" between the two states.
One day before Lukashenko's visit, Yeltsin will make an annual address to the Russian parliament in which he is expected to raise the issue of holding simultaneous referendums on closer integration.
On Sunday several thousand demonstrators gathered in Minsk to protest against Lukashenko's pro-Russian policies.
